flawed_step: Step 5: independence of N(v) does not imply that its vertices use at most three colours in a 4-colouring of G-v.
counterexample: Let C5 be the 5-cycle and M(H) the Mycielski graph of H. Then M(M(C5)) is triangle-free and has chromatic number 5, so it is not 4-colourable.
assessment_summary:
1. Let G be an arbitrary finite triangle-free graph. — JUSTIFIED: This is the correct setup for proving the universal statement.
2. Attempt induction on |V(G)|, with graphs on at most four vertices as the base case. — JUSTIFIED: Such graphs are trivially 4-colourable.
3. Delete a vertex v; the resulting graph G-v is triangle-free and hence, by the induction hypothesis, has a proper 4-colouring. — JUSTIFIED: Vertex deletion cannot create a triangle, and |V(G-v)|<|V(G)|.
4. The neighbourhood N(v) is an independent set. — JUSTIFIED: Two adjacent neighbours of v would form a K3 with v.
5. Therefore the vertices of N(v) use at most three colours in the chosen colouring of G-v. — NOT JUSTIFIED: An independent set can contain vertices of all four colours; independence only says that its members are pairwise nonadjacent.
6. Choose a colour absent from N(v) and assign it to v. — NOT JUSTIFIED: Step 5 does not establish that an absent colour exists.
7. This assignment would extend the colouring properly if such an absent colour existed. — JUSTIFIED CONDITIONALLY: Every edge incident with v would then have differently coloured endpoints, but the required colour was not obtained.
8. Hence the induction proves that every triangle-free graph is 4-colourable. — NOT JUSTIFIED: The induction step fails at Step 5.
9. To determine whether this is merely a defective proof or a false statement, take C5. It is triangle-free and has chromatic number 3. — JUSTIFIED: It contains no three mutually adjacent vertices; its odd cycle prevents a 2-colouring, while colours 1,2,1,2,3 give a proper 3-colouring.
10. For a graph H with vertices x1,...,xn, define M(H) to have vertices x1,...,xn, y1,...,yn, and z; retain every edge xixj of H, add yixj and yjxi for every edge xixj of H, and add zyi for every i. — JUSTIFIED: This explicitly defines the Mycielski construction as a finite simple graph.
11. If H is triangle-free, then M(H) is triangle-free. — JUSTIFIED: A triangle containing z would require an edge between two y-vertices, but none exist. A triangle not containing z has at most one y-vertex; with none it would be a triangle in H, and with yi,xj,xk it would imply that xi,xj,xk form a triangle in H.
12. If χ(H)=k, then M(H) is (k+1)-colourable. — JUSTIFIED: Give each yi the colour of xi in a proper k-colouring of H and give z a new colour; every defined edge then has differently coloured endpoints.
13. If χ(H)=k, then M(H) is not k-colourable. — JUSTIFIED: Suppose it had a k-colouring and rename the colour of z as k. No yi has colour k. On the original copy of H, replace the colour of each xi having colour k by the colour of yi. For an edge xixj, at most one endpoint originally has colour k; if xi does, then yi is adjacent to xj, so the replacement colours remain different. This produces a proper (k-1)-colouring of H, contradicting χ(H)=k.
14. Consequently χ(M(H))=χ(H)+1, and applying the construction twice to C5 gives a triangle-free graph G=M(M(C5)) with χ(G)=5. — JUSTIFIED: Steps 11–13 preserve triangle-freeness and increase the chromatic number from 3 to 4 and then to 5.
15. This G is not 4-colourable. — JUSTIFIED: A graph of chromatic number 5 admits no proper colouring with four colours.
16. Therefore the statement “Every triangle-free graph is 4-colourable” is false. — JUSTIFIED: Step 15 supplies a finite simple triangle-free counterexample.
